title: Module Header: Imports and Proof Architecture
content:
The module imports five Mathlib modules that together provide the complete group-theoretic and field-theoretic infrastructure:

- `Mathlib.FieldTheory.AbelRuffini`: `IsSolvableByRad` and `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` — the bridge from radical solvability to group solvability
- `Mathlib.GroupTheory.Solvable`: `IsSolvable`, `solvable_of_ker_le_range` — the core solvability predicate and exact-sequence theorem
- `Mathlib.GroupTheory.SpecificGroups.Alternating`: `alternatingGroup`, `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` — the A₅ simplicity theorem
- `Mathlib.FieldTheory.Galois.Basic`: `IsGalois`, `card_aut_eq_finrank` — Galois extensions and the fundamental theorem
- `Mathlib.GroupTheory.Perm.Sign`: `Equiv.Perm.sign` — the sign homomorphism $S_n \to \mathbb{Z}^\times$ whose kernel is $A_n$

The module docstring outlines a 15-section structure across 534 lines, providing the complete solvability classification absent from the simpler `AbelRuffini.lean` (185 lines). The `open Equiv Polynomial` declaration avoids namespace prefixes throughout.

This file is the **complement** to `AbelRuffini.lean`: where that file uses the non-solvability of $S_5$ as a black box from Mathlib, this file proves the complete theorem $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ from scratch, explicitly handling each degree and the small-$n$ cases that Mathlib did not provide instances for.
mathContext: The five imports form a hierarchy: `AbelRuffini` sits at the top (field theory + group theory interface), built on `Solvable` (group theory predicate), `Alternating` (specific groups), `Galois.Basic` (field theory), and `Perm.Sign` (the sign homomorphism $\text{sgn}: S_n \to \{\pm 1\}$). The sign homomorphism is the keystone: its kernel $\ker(\text{sgn}) = A_n$ connects the abstract alternating group to the exact sequences used throughout.

title: Trivial and Abelian Base Cases: S₀–S₂ and A₀–A₃
content:
The solvability proofs for the smallest groups use the simplest possible arguments. S₀ and S₁ are trivial (unique element — `isSolvable_of_subsingleton`). S₂ is abelian: `decide` verifies commutativity by exhaustive computation over the 4 elements, then `isSolvable_of_comm` upgrades commutativity to solvability. A₀–A₂ are instances (Mathlib derives solvability automatically since they are subgroups of solvable S₀–S₂). A₃ is the cyclic group of order 3 — `decide` confirms commutativity on 9 element pairs, yielding `isSolvable_of_comm`. The ℤˣ solvability instance (last line of this range) prepares for the S₃ exact sequence: the sign homomorphism maps to ℤˣ, which must be solvable as the codomain.

**Why these 'trivial' base cases are structurally essential, not vacuous.** The seven instances established in lines 49–93 ($S_0, S_1, S_2, A_0, A_1, A_2, A_3$ solvable, plus $\mathbb{Z}^\times$ solvable) are *not* mere bookkeeping — they are the load-bearing inductive anchors for every downstream argument in the file. **(1) `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` at the sharp threshold (Part II, `symmetric_solvable_of_le_four`)** depends on having each of $S_0, S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4$ as a registered `IsSolvable` instance — remove any one and the tactic fails with 'instance not found.' The five-element case split is the *only* way Mathlib's typeclass mechanism can discharge a finite biconditional for a class-level predicate. **(2) The `solvable_of_ker_le_range` extension lemma (used 3 times: $S_3$, $A_4$, $S_4$)** requires solvability of *both* kernel and codomain — the $\mathbb{Z}^\times$ instance here is precisely the codomain hypothesis for the sign sequence $1 \to A_n \to S_n \to \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$ at every $n$. Without `instance : IsSolvable ℤˣ`, the entire small-symmetric-groups chain collapses at the very first extension. **(3) Cumulative structural fact**: every group of order $\leq 3$ is abelian, every group of order $4$ has structure either $\mathbb{Z}/4$ or Klein four — both abelian — so $A_4$ (order 12) is the *minimum order* for a non-abelian alternating group, exactly where the structural argument shifts from `isSolvable_of_comm` (lines 49–93) to the Klein-four normal subgroup construction (lines 105–141). The transition between these two annotation ranges marks the *qualitative* boundary in the file: below it, solvability is automatic from commutativity; above it, the derived series must be tracked explicitly.

**Tactic mechanics — why `decide` works for $S_2$ commutativity but not $A_5$ simplicity.** The `decide` tactic in Lean 4 reduces a decidable proposition to its `Bool` value via kernel evaluation. For $S_2$ commutativity, the proposition `∀ a b : Equiv.Perm (Fin 2), a * b = b * a` reduces to checking $|S_2|^2 = 4$ pairs — trivially fast in the kernel. For $A_3$ commutativity, the same pattern with $|A_3|^2 = 9$ pairs. The boundary where `decide` becomes infeasible and `native_decide` is required arrives at $|A_4|^2 = 144$ for the Klein-four-normality check (line 117 of the source, using `native_decide`), and definitively at $|S_5|^2 = 14400$ for the $S_5$ non-commutativity witness (line 444, also `native_decide`). The choice of `decide` here for $S_2$ and $A_3$ is *not* a style preference — it is the largest tactical primitive whose kernel-time evaluation budget the small-group reductions can afford, and it is the cleanest possible certificate of commutativity in Lean (a single keyword, no algebraic manipulation required). The pattern `decide` + `isSolvable_of_comm` is the canonical Lean idiom for 'this group is small enough to verify commutativity exhaustively, hence solvable' — a pattern that does not generalize to larger non-abelian groups but is *tight* exactly where it works.

**Connection to the Wedderburn small-group catalog.** The seven base cases here ($S_0, S_1, S_2, A_0, A_1, A_2, A_3$) are exhaustively cataloged in the **small-group encyclopedia** (Burnside 1897, Coxeter-Moser 1957, GAP `SmallGroups` library 1999–): every isomorphism class of group of order $\leq 4$ is one of the trivial group, $\mathbb{Z}/2, \mathbb{Z}/3, \mathbb{Z}/4$, Klein four $V_4 \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ — all abelian. The first non-abelian group is $S_3$ at order 6, and the file's `s3_not_comm` (Part XIII, line 437) provides the formal Lean certificate of this fact. The structural reason: any group of order $p$ for prime $p$ is cyclic (Lagrange), any group of order $p^2$ is abelian (a classical theorem from the center being non-trivial in $p$-groups), and order 4 = $2^2$ is the only $p^2$ case below order 6. The file's progression from `isSolvable_of_comm` (orders $\leq 3$) through Klein-four construction ($A_4$, order 12) to the simple $A_5$ (order 60) traces the *small-group classification frontier* one structural level at a time, with each annotation in this file pinned to one level of complexity.

title: Part VI: Subgroup Solvability via Typeclass Inheritance
content:
The `SubgroupSolvability` section (Part VI) proves that subgroups of solvable groups are solvable using `inferInstance` — a one-line proof delegating entirely to Mathlib's typeclass system. This works because Mathlib declares `IsSolvable H` as an automatically derivable instance whenever `H : Subgroup G` and `[IsSolvable G]`: the derived series of $H$ is contained in the derived series of $G$ ($H^{(k)} \leq G^{(k)}$ for all $k$), so the termination of $G^{(\cdot)}$ at $\{e\}$ forces $H^{(\cdot)}$ to terminate too.

This theorem is used implicitly throughout the file. In Part VII, `alternating_solvable_of_le_four` invokes `inferInstance` to conclude $A_n$ solvable from $S_n$ solvable (since $A_n \leq S_n$). The Galois correspondence amplifies this: if the full Galois group is solvable, every intermediate field's Galois group (a subgroup of the full group) is automatically solvable — a key step in building the radical tower.

The `inferInstance` proof style is characteristic of well-designed algebraic hierarchies in Lean: when the inheritance rules are correctly set up in Mathlib, structural properties propagate automatically, turning multi-paragraph proofs into single-keyword proofs. Compare this to the four-lemma proof that would be required without the typeclass infrastructure.
mathContext: $H \leq G$, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow H$ solvable. Derived series: $H^{(0)} = H$, $H^{(k+1)} = [H^{(k)}, H^{(k)}]$. Since $H^{(k)} \leq G^{(k)}$ for all $k$ (by induction: $[H^{(k)}, H^{(k)}] \leq [G^{(k)}, G^{(k)}]$), and $G^{(n)} = \{e\}$ for some $n$ (solvability of $G$), we get $H^{(n)} \leq G^{(n)} = \{e\}$, so $H$ is solvable.

title: Complete A_n Classification: Solvable ↔ n ≤ 4
content:
The complete solvability classification for alternating groups mirrors the symmetric group case. `alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le` proves A_n not solvable for n ≥ 5 by contradiction: if A_n were solvable, then the exact sequence $1 \to A_n \to S_n \to \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$ would give S_n solvable (via `solvable_of_ker_le_range`), contradicting `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le`. The positive direction `alternating_solvable_of_le_four` uses that A_n is a subgroup of S_n for n ≤ 4, and subgroups of solvable groups are solvable. The biconditional `alternating_solvable_iff` assembles these by contradiction with `push_neg` and `omega`.

**Why the $A_n$ classification mirrors the $S_n$ classification exactly.** The biconditionals `symmetric_solvable_iff` and `alternating_solvable_iff` give the *same* threshold $n \leq 4$ — a strong structural fact that requires both directions of the equivalence between $S_n$ solvability and $A_n$ solvability. The short exact sequence $1 \to A_n \to S_n \to \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \to 1$ supplies both directions because $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is abelian (hence solvable): (i) **$A_n$ solvable $\Rightarrow$ $S_n$ solvable** — since $A_n$ (normal subgroup, solvable) and $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ (quotient, abelian) are both solvable, the extension closure (`solvable_of_solvable_normal_quotient` / `solvable_of_ker_le_range` in Mathlib) yields $S_n$ solvable; (ii) **$S_n$ solvable $\Rightarrow$ $A_n$ solvable** — since $A_n \leq S_n$ is a subgroup, the subgroup closure (`subgroup_solvable_of_solvable`) descends solvability from $S_n$ to $A_n$. Combining (i) and (ii): $A_n$ solvable $\iff S_n$ solvable, and the threshold proved here at $n = 4$ is the unique boundary common to both. This is *not* an automatic consequence of the alternating-group definition — it depends critically on the small index $[S_n : A_n] = 2$ (the smallest possible non-trivial index), which forces the quotient $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ to be solvable. For larger normal subgroups with non-abelian quotients, the analogous equivalence fails.

**Why $A_5$ is the *minimal* obstruction in the alternating tower (not $A_n$ for some larger $n$).** The pattern $A_2, A_3, A_4$ all solvable yet $A_5$ not solvable is sharp at $n = 5$ for a specific structural reason: $A_5$ is the smallest non-abelian simple group, and the chain $A_2 = \{e\}$, $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$, $A_4 \supset V_4 \supset \{e\}$ exhibits abelian composition factors at every level before $n = 5$. At $n = 5$, the composition series of $A_5$ collapses to just $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_5$ with a single non-abelian simple factor $A_5/\{e\} = A_5$ — the derived series $A_5^{(0)} = A_5$, $A_5^{(1)} = [A_5, A_5] = A_5$ (since $A_5$ is perfect), $A_5^{(2)} = A_5$, ... never reaches $\{e\}$. This is the *unique* non-solvable obstruction in the chain, in the precise sense that $A_5$ is the only non-abelian simple group of order $< 168$ (the next is $\mathrm{PSL}(2, 7) \cong \mathrm{GL}(3, 2)$ at order 168). For $n \geq 6$, $A_n$ remains non-solvable but for a derivative reason: $A_n$ contains $A_5$ as a subgroup (via the natural embedding $A_5 \hookrightarrow A_n$ fixing $\{6, \ldots, n\}$), so subgroup-closure of solvability (contrapositive direction) propagates non-solvability up. This makes $A_5$ the unique structural witness — every $A_n$ for $n \geq 5$ inherits non-solvability from the same $A_5$ obstruction.

**Tactic mechanics: the `push_neg`/`omega` pattern.** The biconditional `alternating_solvable_iff : IsSolvable (alternatingGroup (Fin n)) ↔ n ≤ 4` is closed by case-analysis on the contrapositive: assume `¬ (n ≤ 4)`, apply `push_neg` to extract `5 ≤ n` from the negated $\leq$, then `omega` discharges the arithmetic to invoke `alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le`. The `push_neg` tactic normalizes negations of arithmetic comparisons (`¬ (n ≤ 4)` becomes `5 ≤ n`), and `omega` is Lean's decision procedure for linear integer arithmetic. This three-line tactic pattern (`intro h; push_neg at h; omega`) is the canonical idiom for symmetric `iff` proofs where the negative direction is a known non-solvability theorem; it appears verbatim in `symmetric_solvable_iff` (Part II) and `alternating_solvable_iff` (Part III), making the architectural parallel between the two biconditionals explicit at the Lean level.
mathContext:
$A_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$. Key step: $A_n \trianglelefteq S_n$ with $S_n/A_n \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. If $A_n$ solvable, then from $1 \to A_n \to S_n \to \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \to 1$, $S_n$ is solvable (solvability extension). Contradiction for $n \geq 5$ since $S_n$ is not solvable.

**Derived series for small $A_n$:** $A_0 = A_1 = A_2 = \{e\}$ (trivial, derived length 0); $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ (abelian, derived length 1, since $[A_3, A_3] = \{e\}$); $A_4$: derived series $A_4 \triangleright V_4 \triangleright \{e\}$ (derived length 2, since $V_4 = [A_4, A_4]$ is abelian and $[V_4, V_4] = \{e\}$); $A_5$ and beyond: $A_n^{(k)} = A_n$ for all $k \geq 0$ (perfect groups, infinite derived length). Compare with $S_n$ derived lengths: $\text{dl}(S_2) = 1$, $\text{dl}(S_3) = 2$, $\text{dl}(S_4) = 3$, $\text{dl}(S_n) = \infty$ for $n \geq 5$. The difference $\text{dl}(S_n) - \text{dl}(A_n) = 1$ for $n \in \{2, 3, 4\}$ reflects the $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ sign-quotient adding one commutator layer; both stabilize at $\infty$ for $n \geq 5$.

**Connection to the Mathlib subgroup chain.** The proof uses `subgroupOf_isSolvable` (or `IsSolvable.subgroupOf`) to descend solvability from $S_n$ to $A_n$ via the inclusion $A_n \hookrightarrow S_n$. Mathlib's `Subgroup` API makes the alternating-group-as-subgroup-of-symmetric-group view machine-checked: `alternatingGroup (Fin n) ≤ Equiv.Perm (Fin n)` is the implicit type-coercion that `subgroupOf` uses, and the solvability closure under subgroups follows from the derived series being preserved under inclusion ($H^{(k)} \leq G^{(k)}$ for $H \leq G$).

title: Solvability Preservation: Subgroups, Quotients, Isomorphisms — and the Schur-Zassenhaus Converse
content:
Part IX (lines 330–347) establishes two structural closure properties that complete the solvability toolkit.

**`quotient_solvable_of_solvable`** (lines 337–339): quotient groups of solvable groups are solvable, proved by `inferInstance`. Mathlib's typeclass system automatically derives `IsSolvable (G ⧸ N)` from `[IsSolvable G]` — the derived series of $G/N$ is the image of the derived series of $G$ under the quotient map, so termination of $G^{(\cdot)}$ implies termination of $(G/N)^{(\cdot)}$.

**`solvable_of_mul_equiv`** (lines 342–345): isomorphic groups share solvability. The proof uses `solvable_of_surjective e.surjective` where `e : G ≃* H` — surjective group homomorphisms preserve solvability (the image of a derived series is a derived series for the image).

Together with subgroup solvability (Part VI, `subgroup_solvable_of_solvable`, lines 237–248), these three closure properties — subgroups, quotients, isomorphisms — make solvability a robust hereditary invariant under the Galois correspondence: if the Galois group of a field extension is solvable, every intermediate extension has a solvable Galois group (subgroup closure), and every quotient extension (corresponding to a normal subgroup) also has a solvable Galois group (quotient closure). The specific non-solvability witnesses for $S_5$–$S_8$ and $A_6$–$A_7$ are in Part XI (lines 366–405).

**Concrete derived-series proofs for each closure property.** The `inferInstance`/`solvable_of_surjective` one-liners in the Lean source compress three distinct derived-series arguments, each worth making explicit.

*(1) Subgroup closure* (`H ≤ G`, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow$ $H$ solvable). The inclusion $H \hookrightarrow G$ sends the commutator $[h_1, h_2] = h_1 h_2 h_1^{-1} h_2^{-1}$ in $H$ to the commutator $[h_1, h_2]$ in $G$ — *the same group element*, just viewed inside the larger group. So $H^{(1)} = [H, H] \leq [G, G] = G^{(1)}$, and by induction $H^{(k)} \leq G^{(k)}$ for all $k$. If $G^{(n)} = \{e\}$ for some $n$ (solvability of $G$), then $H^{(n)} \leq \{e\}$, so $H^{(n)} = \{e\}$ and $H$ is solvable. The derived length of $H$ satisfies $\text{dl}(H) \leq \text{dl}(G)$.

*(2) Quotient closure* (`N ⊴ G`, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow$ $G/N$ solvable). The quotient map $\pi : G \twoheadrightarrow G/N$ sends $[g_1, g_2] \mapsto [\pi(g_1), \pi(g_2)]$, so $\pi([G, G]) = [G/N, G/N]$ and by induction $\pi(G^{(k)}) = (G/N)^{(k)}$. If $G^{(n)} = \{e\}$, then $(G/N)^{(n)} = \pi(G^{(n)}) = \pi(\{e\}) = \{eN\}$, so $G/N$ is solvable with $\text{dl}(G/N) \leq \text{dl}(G)$.

*(3) Isomorphism closure* (`G ≅ H`, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow$ $H$ solvable). An isomorphism $\varphi : G \to H$ is in particular surjective, and the surjection version (Mathlib's `solvable_of_surjective`) gives $H^{(k)} = \varphi(G^{(k)})$. The Lean proof `e.surjective` extracts the surjective component of `e : G ≃* H` and applies the more general theorem; the isomorphism closure is then a special case of the *image* of a solvable group being solvable.

The Lean tactic `inferInstance` succeeds because Mathlib registers each of these as a typeclass instance: `instance : IsSolvable (G ⧸ N)` is derived automatically from `[IsSolvable G]` and `[N.Normal]`. The user-facing one-liners in Part IX simply expose these instances as named theorems for direct citation.

**The Schur-Zassenhaus converse — when does the extension reverse?** The three preservation theorems all go *forward* (solvability descends from $G$ to subgroups, quotients, and isomorphic images), but the *converse* direction — building solvability of $G$ from solvability of $N$ and $G/N$ — is the content of the **solvability extension theorem** (used three times in the small-groups section as `solvable_of_ker_le_range`): if $N \trianglelefteq G$ with both $N$ and $G/N$ solvable, then $G$ is solvable. This is *not* automatic for arbitrary extensions $1 \to N \to G \to Q \to 1$ — it relies on the specific structure that the derived series of $G$ can be reassembled from the derived series of $N$ and $Q$.

The **Schur-Zassenhaus theorem** (Schur 1904, Zassenhaus 1937) sharpens this for *coprime-order* extensions: if $N \trianglelefteq G$ with $\gcd(|N|, |G/N|) = 1$, then the extension *splits* — $G = N \rtimes Q$ where $Q \leq G$ is a complement isomorphic to $G/N$. Combined with the solvability extension theorem and the Feit-Thompson theorem (odd-order groups are solvable), Schur-Zassenhaus gives a powerful structural decomposition: every finite group has a unique *Hall* $\pi$-subgroup for each prime set $\pi$ when the group is solvable, by repeated application of the Schur-Zassenhaus splitting at coprime levels of the composition series. Mathlib formalizes Schur-Zassenhaus as `Sylow.exists_subgroup_card_pow_prime` (the Sylow special case) and `IsPSolvable.schurZassenhaus` (the general version, partial), but the full coprime-order version is not yet in Mathlib as of 2026.

**Concrete usage of all three closures in this file.** The three preservation theorems are not just abstract — they are the *workhorses* of the entire classification:

- **Subgroup closure** is invoked implicitly in Part VII (`alternating_solvable_of_le_four`, lines 281–286) to derive $A_n$ solvability for $n \leq 4$ from $S_n$ solvability. The `inferInstance` proof there delegates to the subgroup-closure typeclass: $A_n \leq S_n$, $S_n$ solvable, therefore $A_n$ solvable.
- **Quotient closure** is the *positive* direction of the solvability extension theorem (a quotient of a solvable group is solvable, hence in any solvability extension $1 \to N \to G \to Q \to 1$ with $G$ solvable, both $N$ and $Q$ are solvable — the *necessary* condition that the small-groups section *partially inverts* via the cocycle structure).
- **Isomorphism closure** is the rigidity backbone: when Mathlib proves $A_n \cong \ker(\text{sign})$ or $S_n / A_n \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, the solvability of one side automatically transfers to the other without re-proof.

**Galois-correspondence amplification.** Under the Galois correspondence, the three closures translate into field-theoretic statements about radical solvability:

- **Subgroup ↔ intermediate field**: if $\text{Gal}(L/K)$ is solvable, then for any intermediate $K \subseteq M \subseteq L$, the Galois group $\text{Gal}(L/M)$ (a subgroup of $\text{Gal}(L/K)$) is solvable — so $L/M$ is solvable by radicals over $M$.
- **Normal subgroup ↔ Galois subextension**: if $\text{Gal}(L/K)$ is solvable and $M/K$ is itself Galois (corresponding to a *normal* subgroup $\text{Gal}(L/M) \trianglelefteq \text{Gal}(L/K)$), then $\text{Gal}(M/K) \cong \text{Gal}(L/K) / \text{Gal}(L/M)$ is a *quotient* — solvable by quotient closure — so $M/K$ is also solvable by radicals.
- **Isomorphism ↔ field equivalence**: if $L/K$ and $L'/K'$ have isomorphic Galois groups (via a compatible field isomorphism $K \to K'$, $L \to L'$), they have the same radical-solvability status. This is the algebraic content of 'the radical-solvability question is a property of the Galois group, not the specific polynomial.'

The three preservation theorems thus make explicit that the Galois-theoretic obstruction proved later in the file (the non-solvability of $S_n$ for $n \geq 5$) propagates uniformly: it blocks radical solvability *at every level* of any extension whose Galois group contains a non-solvable composition factor. The hereditary structure is what makes the threshold $n = 4$ a *global* obstruction rather than an isolated counterexample.

Key facts: (1) $H \leq G$, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow H$ solvable (derived series of $H$ is contained in that of $G$: $H^{(k)} \leq G^{(k)}$ for all $k$). (2) $N \trianglelefteq G$, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow G/N$ solvable (image of derived series under quotient map: $(G/N)^{(k)} = \pi(G^{(k)})$). (3) $\varphi : G \twoheadrightarrow H$ surjective, $G$ solvable $\Rightarrow H$ solvable ($H^{(k)} = \varphi(G^{(k)})$). All three give $\text{dl}(\text{image}) \leq \text{dl}(G)$.

**Solvability extension theorem** (the *converse* direction, used as `solvable_of_ker_le_range`): if $N \trianglelefteq G$ with both $N$ and $G/N$ solvable, then $G$ is solvable. Proof: derived series of $G$ stabilizes once $G^{(k)} \leq N$ (by quotient solvability), then descends to $\{e\}$ inside $N$ (by $N$ solvability). Quantitative form: $\text{dl}(G) \leq \text{dl}(N) + \text{dl}(G/N)$ — exactly the inequality used in the $S_4$ chain $\text{dl}(S_4) \leq \text{dl}(V_4) + \text{dl}(A_4/V_4) + \text{dl}(S_4/A_4) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3$.

**Schur-Zassenhaus theorem** (Schur 1904, Zassenhaus 1937): if $N \trianglelefteq G$ with $\gcd(|N|, |G/N|) = 1$, then $G \cong N \rtimes (G/N)$ — the extension splits and complements are unique up to conjugacy. Combined with the solvability extension theorem and Feit-Thompson (odd-order $\Rightarrow$ solvable), this gives the structural decomposition of finite solvable groups into Hall $\pi$-subgroups. Not fully in Mathlib 2026 (only the Sylow special case `Sylow.exists_subgroup_card_pow_prime`).

**Closure typeclass instances in Mathlib** (so `inferInstance` succeeds): `instance : IsSolvable (G ⧸ N)` (auto from `[IsSolvable G] [N.Normal]`); `instance subgroup_solvable_of_solvable : IsSolvable H` (auto from `H : Subgroup G` and `[IsSolvable G]`); `solvable_of_surjective : Function.Surjective (φ : G →* H) → [IsSolvable G] → IsSolvable H`.

title: S₃ Solvability via Short Exact Sequence
content:
S₃ is proved solvable using the short exact sequence $1 \to A_3 \to S_3 \xrightarrow{\text{sign}} \mathbb{Z}^\times \to 1$. The Lean proof uses `solvable_of_ker_le_range`: if the kernel of a group homomorphism is solvable (here $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$, cyclic, proved solvable by commutativity) and the codomain is solvable ($\mathbb{Z}^\times \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, commutative), then the domain is solvable. This is the solvability extension theorem for group extensions.

**Connection to the derived series**: The composition series $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_3 \trianglelefteq S_3$ coincides with the derived (commutator) series of $S_3$: $S_3^{(1)} = [S_3, S_3] = A_3$ (the commutator subgroup of $S_3$ is exactly $A_3$), and $S_3^{(2)} = [A_3, A_3] = \{e\}$ since $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ is abelian. Hence $S_3$ has **derived length 2** — one step shorter than $S_4$'s derived length 3 (see the $V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4$ annotation). This is the precise group-theoretic reason Cardano's cubic formula needs exactly **two** nested layers of root extraction, where Ferrari's quartic needs three.

**Cardano's two-layer tower (the Lagrange-resolvent face)**: The two abelian quotients $S_3/A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ and $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ correspond to the two radical layers in Cardano's formula. For a cubic $t^3 + pt + q$ with roots $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$, the discriminant square root $\delta = (\alpha_1 - \alpha_2)(\alpha_1 - \alpha_3)(\alpha_2 - \alpha_3)$ satisfies $\delta^2 = \Delta = -4p^3 - 27q^2 \in \mathbb{Q}$; every odd permutation sends $\delta \mapsto -\delta$ while $A_3$ fixes it, so $\mathbb{Q}(\delta) = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{\Delta})$ is precisely the fixed field of $A_3$ — the **$\mathbb{Z}/2$ layer (first square root)**. Over $\mathbb{Q}(\delta, \omega)$ (adjoining a primitive cube root of unity $\omega$), the residual $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ symmetry is resolved by the **Lagrange resolvent** $L = \alpha_1 + \omega\alpha_2 + \omega^2\alpha_3$, whose cube $L^3$ is fixed by $A_3$ and hence rational over the base — taking its cube root is the **$\mathbb{Z}/3$ layer (second, cube root)**. Inverting the linear system in $L$, $\bar L = \alpha_1 + \omega^2\alpha_2 + \omega\alpha_3$, and $\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 + \alpha_3 = 0$ recovers the three roots. Thus the abstract sequence `solvable_of_ker_le_range` constructs here is the algorithmic skeleton of Cardano (1545) — cross-referenced to the gallery entry `solution-of-cubic`.

title: Klein Four-Group and A₄ Solvability
content:
A₄ is proved solvable via the Klein four-group $V_4 = \{e, (12)(34), (13)(24), (14)(23)\}$. The Lean proof defines $V_4$ as the set of elements $x$ in $A_4$ satisfying $x^2 = e$, proves $V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4$ (by `native_decide`), and uses the short exact sequence $1 \to V_4 \to A_4 \to A_4/V_4 \to 1$. Both $V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ (abelian) and $A_4/V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ (cyclic) are solvable. This construction is the only way to prove $A_4$ solvable — $A_4$ itself is non-abelian.

**Connection to the derived series**: The composition series $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$ coincides exactly with the derived (commutator) series of $S_4$: $S_4^{(1)} = [S_4, S_4] = A_4$, $S_4^{(2)} = [A_4, A_4] = V_4$, $S_4^{(3)} = [V_4, V_4] = \{e\}$. This means $S_4$ has **derived length 3**: it takes exactly 3 commutator steps to reach the trivial group. This is the deepest solvable case — among symmetric groups, $S_4$ has the longest derived series. The derived length 3 corresponds to 3 nested levels of root extraction in Cardano's quartic formula.

**$V_4$ as Ferrari's resolvent**: The Klein four-group $V_4$ is *not* an arbitrary normal subgroup — it is the **kernel of $S_4$ acting on the three pairs of opposite edges of a tetrahedron**, equivalently the kernel of the action on the three Lagrange resolvents $\beta_1 = (\alpha_1 + \alpha_2)(\alpha_3 + \alpha_4)$, $\beta_2 = (\alpha_1 + \alpha_3)(\alpha_2 + \alpha_4)$, $\beta_3 = (\alpha_1 + \alpha_4)(\alpha_2 + \alpha_3)$ formed from the four roots of a quartic. The three permutations $(12)(34)$, $(13)(24)$, $(14)(23)$ — the non-identity elements of $V_4$ — are precisely those that fix all three $\beta_i$, so $V_4$ is the kernel of the homomorphism $S_4 \to S_3$ given by the action on $\{\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3\}$. This induces $S_4/V_4 \cong S_3$ (order $24/4 = 6$) — the **resolvent cubic** of Ferrari's quartic formula. The numerical match is exact: Ferrari's reduction sends a degree-4 problem to a degree-3 problem (the resolvent cubic in $\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3$), which Cardano then solves; the algebraic content of this reduction is the surjection $S_4 \twoheadrightarrow S_3$ with kernel $V_4$ that the Lean proof constructs as a normal subgroup.

Derived series of $S_4$: $S_4 \supset A_4 = [S_4,S_4] \supset V_4 = [A_4,A_4] \supset \{e\} = [V_4,V_4]$. title: S₄ Solvability via Exact Sequence 1 → A₄ → S₄ → ℤˣ → 1
content:
`perm_fin_4_solvable` is proved by `solvable_of_ker_le_range` applied to the sign homomorphism: the kernel inclusion $A_4 \hookrightarrow S_4$ witnesses that every element in the kernel of $\text{sign}: S_4 \to \mathbb{Z}^\times$ lies in $A_4$, and $A_4$ is solvable (via the Klein four-group, proved in the preceding lemmas). The proof converts `MonoidHom.mem_ker` evidence directly to membership in the alternating group via `Equiv.Perm.mem_alternatingGroup`. This exact sequence argument is the fourth and most technically involved of the small-group solvability proofs — the `intro x hx; rw [...] ; exact ⟨⟨x, ...⟩, rfl⟩` pattern establishes the kernel containment.

Together with the preceding 12 lemmas (S₀–S₃ and A₀–A₄ solvability), this completes the `SmallSymmetricGroups` section at line 152, establishing all the base cases for the bidirectional solvability theorem.

**The full $S_4$ composition series — the topmost solvable symmetric group.** The proof of `perm_fin_4_solvable` is a *one-step* extension lifting $A_4$ solvability (established by `alternating_fin_4_solvable` at lines 137–141) through the sign sequence. Unfolding the recursion exposes the complete chain that this lemma's solvability rests on: $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$ — the unique composition series of $S_4$, with abelian factors $V_4 \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$ (Klein four-group, the unique non-trivial normal subgroup of $A_4$), $A_4/V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$ (cyclic of order 3, isomorphic to $A_3$), and $S_4/A_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ (cyclic of order 2, generated by the sign). The chain has **derived length 3**: $S_4^{(0)} = S_4$, $S_4^{(1)} = [S_4, S_4] = A_4$, $S_4^{(2)} = [A_4, A_4] = V_4$, $S_4^{(3)} = [V_4, V_4] = \{e\}$. This is the *maximum* derived length among all solvable symmetric groups — $S_3$ has derived length 2, $S_2$ has derived length 1, and $S_5, S_6, \ldots$ have derived length $\infty$ (perfect $A_n$ kernels) — so this single lemma is the *quantitative apex* of the entire solvability classification.

**Why this is the *threshold* lemma.** The structural significance of `perm_fin_4_solvable` is that it is the *last* solvable case before the Abel-Ruffini barrier: $S_5$ is non-solvable because $A_5$ is the smallest non-abelian simple group, blocking any composition series with abelian factors. The chain $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$ is sharply maximal in two senses: (i) **degree-maximal** — no symmetric group above $S_4$ admits a chain with abelian factors, and (ii) **length-maximal** — no solvable symmetric group below $S_4$ requires a chain longer than 3, since the derived length is monotone with $n$ in the solvable range. The proof `perm_fin_4_solvable` thus *occupies* the threshold rather than approaching it: it is simultaneously the apex of the solvable regime and the immediate predecessor of the non-solvable obstruction.

**Correspondence with Ferrari's quartic formula (1540).** The three-layer composition series $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$ matches Ferrari's quartic algorithm step-for-step:

  1. **$S_4/A_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$** (outermost, sign layer) — encodes the **discriminant square root** $\delta(f) = \prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i - \alpha_j)$. Every $\sigma \in S_4$ acts on $\delta$ by $\sigma(\delta) = \text{sgn}(\sigma) \cdot \delta$, so $\delta$ generates the unique quadratic subfield of the splitting field (Galois group $S_4/A_4$). Ferrari's first algebraic step — extracting $\sqrt{\Delta(f)}$ — descends from $\text{Gal} = S_4$ to $\text{Gal} = A_4$.
  2. **$A_4/V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3$** (middle, resolvent-cubic layer) — encodes the **Lagrange resolvent cubic** $R(y) = (y - \alpha_1\alpha_2 - \alpha_3\alpha_4)(y - \alpha_1\alpha_3 - \alpha_2\alpha_4)(y - \alpha_1\alpha_4 - \alpha_2\alpha_3)$ whose three roots are permuted by $A_4$ through its quotient $A_4/V_4$. Ferrari's resolvent cubic — a degree-3 equation in the coefficients of the original quartic — is solved by Cardano's formula (cube root + nested square root), descending from $\text{Gal} = A_4$ to $\text{Gal} = V_4$.
  3. **$V_4 \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$** (innermost, two square-root layer) — encodes the **two square roots** $\sqrt{\alpha_1\alpha_2 - \alpha_3\alpha_4}$ and $\sqrt{\alpha_1\alpha_3 - \alpha_2\alpha_4}$ that, together with the resolvent cubic roots, recover the four original roots $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3, \alpha_4$ via the linear system $V_4 = \ker(A_4 \twoheadrightarrow S_3)$.

The abstract chain $S_4 \twoheadrightarrow S_4/V_4 \cong S_3$ at the level of Galois groups corresponds *exactly* to the algebraic substitution that reduces Ferrari's quartic to a resolvent cubic via the *Tschirnhaus reduction* $m = t - 5p/6$ (formalized in the companion entry `solution-of-cubic-oq-05`). The derived length 3 of $S_4$ is therefore the precise *radical-tower depth* of Ferrari's formula: cube root inside square root inside square root, three nested layers total — and this matches `dl(S_4) = 3` *because* Galois's solvability criterion is a tight bijection between derived-series steps and radical-tower layers.

**Why the proof is technically harder than $S_3$.** Comparing `perm_fin_4_solvable` (lines 144–150, 7 lines) with `perm_fin_3_solvable` (Part I): the $S_3$ case uses a single application of `solvable_of_ker_le_range` with the kernel $A_3$ (which is *abelian*, of order 3, so `isSolvable_of_comm` works directly). The $S_4$ case is structurally identical at the top — `solvable_of_ker_le_range` on the sign sequence — but the kernel $A_4$ is *not* abelian, so its solvability cannot be proved by `isSolvable_of_comm`. Instead, the proof depends on `alternating_fin_4_solvable` (lines 137–141), which itself uses `solvable_of_ker_le_range` *again* with the Klein four-group $V_4$. The two-stage recursion is the structural reason $S_4$ requires the **Klein four-group construction** (lines 105–141, 36 lines of dedicated infrastructure) absent from the $S_3$ proof — and the structural reason no analogous lemma `perm_fin_5_solvable` can exist (any attempted recursion would terminate at $A_5$, which has no non-trivial normal subgroup to extract).

**Why the file does *not* unfold the recursion explicitly.** The proof `perm_fin_4_solvable` lazily invokes `alternating_fin_4_solvable` as a registered instance — Lean's typeclass resolver finds it automatically. This is the right level of abstraction for the *threshold biconditional* (`symmetric_solvable_iff`, see `arg-sharp-threshold`), which uses `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` to discharge all five base cases ($n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$) in a single tactic call. The flat, single-step appearance of `perm_fin_4_solvable` is therefore *deliberate API design*: it lets the threshold biconditional treat $S_4$ uniformly with $S_0, S_1, S_2, S_3$, all dispatched as registered `IsSolvable` instances, even though the underlying $S_4$ proof depth (3 layers) is strictly larger than the others. This contrast — single-line tactic `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` at the threshold versus 36 lines of $V_4$ infrastructure underneath — is the architectural fingerprint of building on Mathlib's typeclass system: complex *proofs* compress to *one-line invocations* once their instances are registered.

**Composition factors and Ferrari's radical-tower depth.** Each composition factor corresponds to one *abelian extension* in Ferrari's quartic formula (1540):

title: The Sharp Solvability Threshold: n ≤ 4
content:
The complete biconditional $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ is the central classification theorem of the file, assembled from two halves that meet exactly at $n = 4$. For $n \leq 4$: `symmetric_solvable_of_le_four` uses `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` to dispatch to the five concrete instances ($n = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$). For $n \geq 5$: `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le` calls Mathlib's `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` after lifting the natural number bound to a cardinal inequality via `Cardinal.mk (Fin n)`. The biconditional `symmetric_solvable_iff` combines these via `by_contra`/`push_neg`/`omega`. The threshold is *sharp* in the strongest possible sense — both directions are tight, and no intermediate value of $n$ exhibits 'partial solvability.'

**What 'sharp' actually means here.** A threshold theorem at $n = 4$ could be sharp in three increasingly strong senses: (i) **directional sharpness** — every $n \leq 4$ is solvable AND every $n \geq 5$ is not, with no exceptions on either side (this file proves both); (ii) **derived-length sharpness** — at $n = 4$ the derived length jumps from 3 (at $S_4$) to infinity (at $S_5$ and beyond), with no intermediate values like 4 or 5 being achieved (this is the deeper qualitative claim, witnessed by the explicit derived series $S_4 \triangleright A_4 \triangleright V_4 \triangleright \{e\}$ of length 3 versus $S_5^{(k)} = S_5$ for all $k \geq 1$ — see `arg-klein-four-a4` for the $S_4$ chain); (iii) **structural sharpness** — the obstruction at $n = 5$ is not an arithmetic accident but is forced by the appearance of $A_5$ as a simple non-abelian composition factor, with $|A_5| = 60$ being exactly the smallest order at which a non-abelian simple group can exist (the smaller candidates of order 4, 6, 8, ..., 59 are all either prime-power or have a non-trivial Sylow subgroup forced to be normal — see the Burnside $p^a q^b$ theorem in the openQuestions, which together with the conjugacy-class arithmetic $\{1, 12, 12, 15, 20\} = 60$ corners $A_5$ as the unique minimal example).

**Tactic mechanics: the `interval_cases <;> infer_instance` idiom.** The forward direction `symmetric_solvable_of_le_four` is *remarkably concise* for what it claims: a single line `interval_cases n <;> infer_instance` proves five separate solvability statements at once. The `interval_cases n` tactic, given the hypothesis `n ≤ 4`, automatically splits the proof into five goals (`n = 0`, `n = 1`, ..., `n = 4`) by case analysis on the natural number range; the `<;>` combinator then applies `infer_instance` to each resulting goal, asking Lean's typeclass resolver to find a registered `IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))` instance for each specific value. Each instance has been registered in Part I of the file: `S_0, S_1` via `isSolvable_of_subsingleton`, $S_2$ via `isSolvable_of_comm` (decide), $S_3$ via `solvable_of_ker_le_range` on the sign sequence, and $S_4$ via the chain through $V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4$. The one-line tactic thus *delegates* to all five Part-I proofs simultaneously — making the architectural point that the forward direction is a direct corollary of the small-cases work, not new content.

**Tactic mechanics: the cardinal-lifting bridge.** The reverse direction `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le` is structurally different because it invokes a *general* Mathlib theorem `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable : 5 ≤ Cardinal.mk α → ¬ IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm α)` that works for any type `α` of cardinality $\geq 5$, not just `Fin n`. To apply this with the natural-number hypothesis `hn : 5 ≤ n`, the proof first builds the cardinal bound `h : 5 ≤ Cardinal.mk (Fin n)` via `simp only [Cardinal.mk_fintype, Fintype.card_fin]` followed by `exact_mod_cast hn`. The two simp lemmas `Cardinal.mk_fintype` (cardinal of a fintype equals its `Fintype.card`) and `Fintype.card_fin` (`Fintype.card (Fin n) = n`) compress the cardinal `Cardinal.mk (Fin n)` to the natural number `n`, and `exact_mod_cast` handles the implicit `Nat → Cardinal` coercion. This three-line bridge is the canonical pattern for invoking Mathlib's type-class-polymorphic theorems with concrete `Fin n` arguments — and it shows that the file's *file-level* `Fin n` indexing is consistent with Mathlib's more general universe-polymorphic approach.

**Tactic mechanics: the `by_contra` biconditional packaging.** The biconditional `symmetric_solvable_iff : IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) ↔ n ≤ 4` packages the two directions via `constructor` followed by two sub-proofs: the *forward* direction (`IsSolvable → n ≤ 4`) is handled by `by_contra`+`push_neg`+`omega` — assume `¬ n ≤ 4`, normalize negation to `5 ≤ n`, then derive contradiction with `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le`. The *backward* direction is `symmetric_solvable_of_le_four` directly. This three-line idiom (`intro h; by_contra hle; push_neg at hle; exact symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le (by omega) h`) is repeated *verbatim* in `alternating_solvable_iff` (Part VII), making the architectural parallel between the two biconditionals explicit at the Lean source level — the *same proof template* works for $S_n$ and $A_n$, indicating that the threshold $n = 4$ is a structural property shared by both groups, not coincidental.

**Connection to the field-theoretic Abel-Ruffini.** The biconditional $S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$ is the *group-theoretic content* that, combined with Galois's solvability criterion (proved separately in this file as `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_galois`, see `arg-galois-contrapositive`) and the *generic polynomial theorem* (van der Waerden 1930: the generic degree-$n$ polynomial over $k(e_1, \ldots, e_n)$ has Galois group $S_n$ — see meta.json keyInsight #13), yields the analytic Abel-Ruffini statement: *the general polynomial of degree $n$ is solvable by radicals if and only if $n \leq 4$*. The threshold theorem in this annotation is therefore the *exact* group-theoretic mirror of the historical impossibility result: $n \leq 4$ corresponds to the *existence* of Cardano (1545) and Ferrari (1540) formulas, and $n \geq 5$ corresponds to Abel's (1824) and Ruffini's (1799) impossibility proofs. The descent from the generic case to specific rational polynomials is **Hilbert's irreducibility theorem** (Hilbert 1892, also formalized as Serre 1992 thin-set version), which guarantees that 'most' rational quintics retain the $S_5$ Galois group of the generic case, so the abstract non-solvability of $S_5$ propagates to concrete unsolvability of specific quintics like Selmer's $x^5 - x - 1$.

**Conceptual subtlety: the threshold is sharp, but the *witnesses* are non-uniform.** While the threshold value $n = 4$ is uniform, the *reason* each side of the threshold holds varies dramatically with $n$. On the solvable side: $S_0, S_1$ are trivial; $S_2$ is abelian; $S_3$ uses a single $\mathbb{Z}/2$ extension over an abelian $A_3$; $S_4$ requires a *three-layer* tower through $V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$. The derived length jumps non-uniformly: $\text{dl}(S_0) = \text{dl}(S_1) = 0$, $\text{dl}(S_2) = 1$, $\text{dl}(S_3) = 2$, $\text{dl}(S_4) = 3$ — each successive value adds *exactly one* commutator step. On the non-solvable side: $S_5, S_6, \ldots$ are all non-solvable for the *same* underlying reason — they all contain $A_5$ as a composition factor (for $S_5$) or as a subgroup that forces non-solvability (for $S_n, n \geq 6$, via subgroup-closure of solvability applied contrapositively). The threshold is sharp not because the obstruction strengthens beyond $n = 5$, but because it *first appears* at $n = 5$ — and once present, propagates upward unchanged. This is the deeper meaning of 'sharp': $n = 5$ is the *initial* value at which the simple non-abelian group $A_5$ enters as an inescapable composition factor.

For $n \geq 5$: `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable (Fin n) h` where `h : 5 ≤ Cardinal.mk (Fin n)` is derived from `5 ≤ n` via `simp [Cardinal.mk_fintype, Fintype.card_fin]`. The cardinal lifting step is the technical mechanism connecting the concrete $n \geq 5$ hypothesis to Mathlib's abstract `Equiv.Perm.not_solvable` (which works for any fintype of cardinality $\geq 5$, not just `Fin n`).

**Derived length values across the threshold.** $\text{dl}(S_n) = \max(0, n - 1)$ for $n \leq 4$: explicitly, $\text{dl}(S_0) = \text{dl}(S_1) = 0$ (trivial), $\text{dl}(S_2) = 1$ ($S_2 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$, $[S_2, S_2] = \{e\}$), $\text{dl}(S_3) = 2$ ($[S_3, S_3] = A_3$, $[A_3, A_3] = \{e\}$), $\text{dl}(S_4) = 3$ ($[S_4, S_4] = A_4$, $[A_4, A_4] = V_4$, $[V_4, V_4] = \{e\}$). For $n \geq 5$: $\text{dl}(S_n) = \infty$ — the derived series stabilizes at $A_n^{(k)} = A_n$ for all $k \geq 1$ since $A_n$ is perfect for $n \geq 5$ (i.e., $[A_n, A_n] = A_n$, a direct consequence of $A_n$'s simplicity for $n \geq 5$ and its non-abelian-ness). The jump from finite $\text{dl} = 3$ at $n = 4$ to $\text{dl} = \infty$ at $n = 5$ is the quantitative form of the threshold's sharpness.

**Generic Galois group bridge to Abel-Ruffini (van der Waerden 1930).** Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$ and let $t_1, \ldots, t_n$ be algebraically independent indeterminates over $k$. The **generic monic polynomial of degree $n$** is $f(X) = \prod_{i=1}^n (X - t_i) = X^n - e_1 X^{n-1} + \cdots + (-1)^n e_n \in k(e_1, \ldots, e_n)[X]$, where $e_j = e_j(t_1, \ldots, t_n)$ is the $j$-th elementary symmetric polynomial. Then $\text{Gal}(k(t_1, \ldots, t_n) / k(e_1, \ldots, e_n)) \cong S_n$, acting by permuting the indeterminate roots $t_i$. Combined with Galois's solvability criterion (char $0$: $f$ solvable by radicals $\iff \text{Gal}(f)$ solvable), this turns the biconditional proved here ($S_n$ solvable $\iff n \leq 4$) into the *analytic* Abel-Ruffini statement: *the general degree-$n$ polynomial is solvable by radicals $\iff n \leq 4$*. The descent to rational polynomials is **Hilbert's irreducibility theorem** (Hilbert 1892, Serre's *Topics in Galois Theory* 1992 §3): specializing the indeterminate coefficients $e_j$ to rational values preserves $\text{Gal} = S_n$ outside a *thin set* of $(e_1, \ldots, e_n) \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ — so 'generic' rational polynomials of degree $n \geq 5$ have Galois group $S_n$ and are unsolvable by radicals.

title: A₅ is Simple and Has Order 60: The Minimal Obstruction
content:
Part III (lines 185–199) establishes two facts about $A_5$ that together make it the minimal obstruction to solvability.

**`a5_simple`** (lines 191–193): $A_5$ is the smallest non-abelian simple group. Its simplicity is the root obstruction to $S_5$'s non-solvability: a solvable group has a composition series with abelian factors, but $A_5$ is simple and non-abelian, so it cannot appear in any such series. Lean invokes `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` from Mathlib. The simplicity of $A_5$ was proved by Galois himself in 1832 and is the centerpiece of the unsolvability proof.

**`card_a5`** (lines 195–197): $|A_5| = 60 = 5!/2$, verified by `decide`. This order is not just a number — it is the **minimum possible order of a non-abelian simple group**. The Feit-Thompson theorem (1963) implies every finite group of odd order is solvable, so any non-abelian simple group must have even order. Among groups of even order $< 60$, all are solvable (every such group has a prime composition factor or is a $p$-group). This makes $A_5$ the unique simple non-abelian group of minimum order, establishing it as the unavoidable obstruction at the exact boundary $n = 4$.

**Burnside's $p^a q^b$ sharpness — why $A_5$ has 60 = $2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$**: Burnside's theorem (1904) proves that every finite group whose order has *at most two* distinct prime divisors is solvable. Therefore no non-abelian simple group can have order $p^a$ (a $p$-group, automatically nilpotent), $p^a q^b$ (Burnside), and certainly not a $p$-group times a prime ($p^a q$). The smallest order with *three* distinct primes is $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 30$; checking $30, 2 \cdot 30 = 60$: every group of order 30 is solvable (Sylow gives a normal subgroup), so 60 is the first achievable order. The factorization $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ shows $A_5$ uses exactly the minimum: two of the three primes appear with multiplicity 1, and only the prime 2 needs multiplicity 2 to escape the order-30 reduction. Burnside's two-prime bound is thus a sharp upper boundary on solvability that $A_5$ exceeds by the smallest possible margin — explaining structurally why the unsolvability threshold falls at $n = 4$ rather than higher.
mathContext: $A_5$ is simple: the only normal subgroups are $\{e\}$ and $A_5$ itself. $|A_5| = 60 = 5!/2$. In the composition series of $S_5$: $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_5 \trianglelefteq S_5$, where $A_5/\{e\} \cong A_5$ is simple and non-abelian. A group is solvable iff all composition factors are cyclic of prime order (equivalently, iff the derived series reaches $\{e\}$). Remarkably, $A_5$ carries three exceptional isomorphisms: $A_5 \cong \text{PSL}(2,4) \cong \text{PSL}(2,5) \cong I$, where $I$ is the icosahedral rotation group (60 orientation-preserving symmetries of the regular icosahedron). These identify $A_5$ as the first member of the $\text{PSL}(2,q)$ family of finite simple groups (simple for prime powers $q \geq 4$). The `decide` tactic verifies $|A_5| = 60$ by exhaustive fintype enumeration — a concrete computational confirmation of the algebraic identity $|A_n| = n!/2$.

title: Galois's Theorem — Contrapositive Form
content:
The key theorem connecting group theory to polynomial solvability: if the Galois group $\text{Gal}(q)$ of an irreducible polynomial $q$ is not solvable, then no root of $q$ is expressible by radicals. This is the contrapositive of Galois's fundamental theorem ($\alpha$ solvable by radicals $\Rightarrow \text{Gal}(q)$ solvable). The Lean proof uses `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` from Mathlib, which formalizes the radical tower construction. Together with $S_5$ not solvable, this proves the general quintic unsolvability.

**Radical tower mechanics**: The Mathlib statement `solvableByRad.isSolvable'` encodes the chain of reasoning: a radical extension $F \subset F(\alpha)$ with $\alpha$ solvable by radicals is built up as a tower $F = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset K_2 \subset \ldots \subset K_n$ where each $K_{i+1} = K_i(\beta_i)$ adjoins a $p_i$-th root $\beta_i^{p_i} \in K_i$ for some prime $p_i$. After adjoining suitable roots of unity, each step's Galois group $\text{Gal}(K_{i+1}/K_i)$ is cyclic of order $p_i$ (Kummer theory). The full Galois group $\text{Gal}(K_n/K_0)$ thus admits a chain of normal subgroups with cyclic prime-order quotients — exactly the definition of solvability. Contrapositively, $\text{Gal}(q)$ non-solvable rules out the existence of any such tower containing a root of $q$.
mathContext: $q$ irreducible, $q(\alpha)=0$, $\text{Gal}(q)$ not solvable $\Rightarrow \alpha \notin F(\text{radicals})$. Formal: `¬IsSolvable q.Gal → ¬IsSolvableByRad F α`. The positive direction (Galois 1832): $\alpha \in F(\text{radicals}) \Rightarrow \text{Gal}(q)$ is solvable, proved via the radical tower $F = K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \ldots \subset K_n \ni \alpha$, $K_{i+1} = K_i(\beta_i)$ with $\beta_i^{p_i} \in K_i$. **Kummer theory** supplies the cyclic-quotient step: if $K$ contains a primitive $p$-th root of unity $\zeta_p$ and $\beta^p = a \in K$, then $K(\beta)/K$ is a cyclic extension of degree dividing $p$, with $\text{Gal}(K(\beta)/K) \hookrightarrow \langle \zeta_p \rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ via $\sigma \mapsto \sigma(\beta)/\beta$. Stacking these cyclic quotients yields a composition series with prime-cyclic factors — the Lean type `IsSolvable q.Gal`.
prerequisites: Kummer theory (cyclic extensions of degree p)

title: Chain Properties: Commutator Solvability, Sign Kernel, and Abelian Factors
content:
The `ChainProperties` section (Part XII) collects three structural results that complete the algebraic picture.

**commutator_solvable** (lines 413–416): In a solvable group $G$, the commutator subgroup $[G, G]$ (generated by all $ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$) is also solvable. In Lean this is `inferInstance` — the typeclass system derives `IsSolvable (commutator G)` automatically because Mathlib registers `Subgroup.isSolvable : [IsSolvable G] → IsSolvable (H : Subgroup G)` and `commutator G = G^{(1)}` is exposed as a `Subgroup G`. The one-line proof is thus a typeclass triangulation: `inferInstance` finds `Subgroup.isSolvable` through `commutator G`'s `Subgroup G` projection. Conceptually this is the algebraic content of the derived series descending: $G^{(1)} \supseteq G^{(2)} \supseteq \ldots \to \{e\}$ for solvable $G$ means the chain from $G^{(1)}$ onward is the *tail* of the same eventually-trivial sequence, so solvability of the head implies solvability of the tail.

**sign_kernel_is_alternating** (lines 418–422): The formal identity $\ker(\mathrm{sgn}) = A_n$ — the file's *keystone lemma*. Mathlib defines `alternatingGroup α := (Equiv.Perm.sign : Equiv.Perm α →* ℤˣ).ker` as a `Subgroup`, so the theorem is essentially the *propositional unfolding* of the definition: `ext x` reduces subgroup equality to a pointwise membership iff, and `simp [MonoidHom.mem_ker, Equiv.Perm.mem_alternatingGroup]` discharges both sides to $\text{sign}(x) = 1$. The value is API: by exposing the kernel ↔ alternating identification as a *named subgroup equality*, downstream proofs can `rw` it directly rather than re-deriving the membership equivalence per element. In this file the kernel-to-alternating bridge is in fact inlined three times (`perm_fin_3_solvable` at lines 102–103, `perm_fin_4_solvable` at lines 148–150, and `alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le` at lines 267–268) — each instance reconstructs the same `MonoidHom.mem_ker` ↦ `Equiv.Perm.mem_alternatingGroup.mpr` two-step locally because those proofs need the *elementwise* witness to feed `solvable_of_ker_le_range`'s pointwise hypothesis. The named theorem packages the *subgroup-level* fact for callers that operate at that abstraction level (e.g., future Galois correspondence proofs that read $A_n$ as $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)^{(1)}$ via the sign character) and is thus the linchpin on which every short-exact-sequence argument in Part I conceptually pivots, even though the tactical proofs unfold the membership equivalence inline.

**solvable_small_has_abelian_factors** (lines 424–428): Packages the result that for $n \leq 4$, both $S_n$ and $A_n$ are simultaneously solvable. The anonymous constructor $\langle \text{symmetric\_solvable\_of\_le\_four } hn,\ \text{alternating\_solvable\_of\_le\_four } hn\rangle$ pairs the two existing solvability witnesses without re-derivation. This conjunction is useful as a single lemma for callers needing both facts — e.g., to construct the canonical $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_n \trianglelefteq S_n$ composition tower for degree $\leq 4$ extensions, where the chain witness requires *both* $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(A_n)$ (to refine the bottom segment via $V_4$ at $n=4$ or via the trivial chain at $n \leq 3$) and $\mathrm{IsSolvable}(S_n)$ (to certify the top quotient $S_n / A_n \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ is abelian, which is automatic from $S_n$ solvability via `IsSolvable.quotient`). Flagged in `meta.originalContributions` as a deliberate API ergonomic — bundling two Mathlib instance inferences into a single citation.

Joint solvability: $n \leq 4 \Rightarrow (S_n \text{ solvable}) \wedge (A_n \text{ solvable})$, with the $V_4$-refined composition factors $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$ giving abelian quotients $V_4,\ A_4/V_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3,\ S_4/A_4 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$ at the boundary case $n = 4$.

title: Non-Commutativity Witnesses via decide/native_decide
content:
Five non-commutativity witnesses (S₃, S₄, S₅, A₄, A₅) are proved by exhibiting specific non-commuting pairs. The proofs use `push_neg` (to turn $\neg \forall a b, ab = ba$ into $\exists a b, ab \neq ba$) followed by `decide` or `native_decide`. This reveals **three distinct structural thresholds** in the symmetric and alternating group families, each marking a different qualitative boundary:

**Threshold 1 — Commutativity (n = 3 for $S_n$, n = 4 for $A_n$)**: $S_1$ and $S_2$ are abelian ($S_2 \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, trivially commutative); $S_3$ is the smallest non-abelian group (order 6). For alternating groups, $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ is still abelian — non-commutativity appears at $A_4$ (order 12). The commutativity threshold is *strictly below* both higher thresholds.

**Threshold 2 — Solvability (n = 5)**: $S_3$, $S_4$, and $A_4$ are *solvable-but-non-abelian* — they are non-commutative but still have composition series with abelian factors ($\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_3 \trianglelefteq S_3$ and $\{e\} \trianglelefteq V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4 \trianglelefteq S_4$). Only at $n = 5$ does non-solvability appear: $S_5$ and $A_5$ are both non-abelian and non-solvable.

**Threshold 3 — Simplicity for $A_n$ (n = 5)**: This is a *distinct* boundary from solvability, even though it coincides numerically at $n = 5$. $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ is simple (as a cyclic group of prime order — but trivially so, being abelian). $A_4$ is **not** simple — its non-trivial normal subgroup $V_4 = \{x \in A_4 : x^2 = e\} \cong (\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$ (constructed in this file via `klein_four`, lines 105–141) is exactly what enables $A_4$'s solvability. $A_5$ is the *first non-abelian simple* group: simple AND non-abelian — the combination that obstructs any abelian-factor composition series. Crucially, the *coincidence* of Thresholds 2 and 3 at $n = 5$ for alternating groups is no accident: $A_n$ simple + $A_n$ non-abelian $\Rightarrow A_n$ non-solvable (a simple non-abelian group has no proper non-trivial normal subgroups, so its only composition factor is itself — which is non-abelian — preventing any abelian-factor refinement). Conversely $A_4$ being solvable forces it to have the non-trivial normal subgroup $V_4$, breaking simplicity.

The split of the five witnesses into solvable-but-non-abelian ($S_3$, $S_4$, $A_4$) and non-solvable-and-non-abelian ($S_5$, $A_5$) makes the boundary $n = 4$ visible directly in the non-commutativity data: all five are non-abelian, but the structural gap between $S_4$ (solvable, $A_4$ non-simple) and $S_5$ (non-solvable, $A_5$ simple) corresponds precisely to the *simultaneous* failure of solvability and the *appearance* of simplicity in $A_n$. This three-threshold hierarchy (commutativity at $n = 3$ for $S_n$ / $n = 4$ for $A_n$; solvability at $n = 5$; simplicity-with-non-abelian-character at $n = 5$ for $A_n$) is the algebraic skeleton beneath the symmetric/alternating classification.

**Concrete witness inventory** (canonical non-commuting pairs, using Lean's `Equiv.Perm` convention $(\sigma \cdot \tau)(x) = \sigma(\tau(x))$): the five `decide`/`native_decide` proofs in the source are non-constructive in the sense that they search over $|G|^2$ pairs without naming the chosen witness, but every search must land on a pair equivalent to one of these canonical witnesses up to conjugation. (i) **$S_3$ — transposition vs. 3-cycle**: take $\sigma = (1\,2)$, $\tau = (1\,2\,3)$. Then $\sigma\tau = (2\,3)$ but $\tau\sigma = (1\,3)$ — both transpositions, but on disjoint pairs. This is the *smallest* witness in any symmetric group: $|S_3| = 6$ with $6^2 = 36$ pairs to check, completed by kernel `decide` in microseconds. (ii) **$S_4$, $S_5$ — same pair, embedded**: the same $\sigma = (1\,2), \tau = (1\,2\,3)$ remain non-commuting in any $S_n$ with $n \geq 3$ (the witness lives in the natural $S_3 \hookrightarrow S_n$ stabilizing $\{4, \ldots, n\}$). The reason `s5_not_comm` needs `native_decide` is not that a different witness is required, but that the decision procedure cannot exploit the embedding — it brute-forces all $120^2 = 14{,}400$ pairs of $S_5$ rather than restricting to the $36$ pairs in the embedded $S_3$. (iii) **$A_4$ — two intersecting 3-cycles**: take $\sigma = (1\,2\,3), \tau = (1\,2\,4)$ (both even, both in $A_4$). Then $\sigma\tau = (1\,3)(2\,4)$ and $\tau\sigma = (1\,4)(2\,3)$ — both *land inside the Klein four-group $V_4$* but are different non-identity elements of $V_4$, giving a concrete instance of the inclusion $[A_4, A_4] = V_4$ (the commutator $[\sigma, \tau] = \sigma\tau\sigma^{-1}\tau^{-1}$ for two intersecting 3-cycles produces a double transposition). (iv) **$A_5$ — two disjoint-support 3-cycles**: take $\sigma = (1\,2\,3), \tau = (3\,4\,5)$ (overlap on the single point $3$). Then $\sigma\tau = (1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$ and $\tau\sigma = (1\,2\,4\,5\,3)$ — two different 5-cycles, witnessing simultaneously (a) non-commutativity in $A_5$, (b) the existence of 5-cycles in $A_5$ (used elsewhere in the file's Sylow structure for `card_a5`), and (c) the closure of $A_5$ under conjugation by 3-cycles (any 5-cycle is conjugate to $(1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$ in $S_5$, but in $A_5$ the 5-cycles split into *two* conjugacy classes of 12 each — a fact used implicitly by `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` via the $\{1, 12, 12, 15, 20\}$ conjugacy-class arithmetic referenced in keyInsight #8). The witness $(1\,2\,3), (3\,4\,5)$ is *also* the canonical generating pair for $A_5$ as a finitely-presented group ($A_5 = \langle a, b \mid a^2 = b^3 = (ab)^5 = e\rangle$ after relabeling), making it the algebraically-minimal certificate of non-commutativity in the minimal non-abelian simple group.
mathContext: Non-commutativity: $\exists a, b \in G$ with $ab \neq ba$. Small cases use `decide` (fintype enumeration over all $|G|^2$ pairs). Larger cases (S₅, A₄, A₅) require `native_decide` for performance ($|S_5|^2 = 14400$ pairs). **Three structural thresholds**: (1) Commutativity — $S_n$ abelian iff $n \leq 2$; $A_n$ abelian iff $n \leq 3$ (since $A_3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$). (2) Solvability — $S_n, A_n$ solvable iff $n \leq 4$. (3) Simplicity-with-non-abelian-character for $A_n$ — $A_n$ is simple non-abelian iff $n \geq 5$ (and $A_4$ has $V_4$ as proper non-trivial normal subgroup, breaking simplicity). The simplicity threshold *coincides* with the solvability threshold at $n = 5$ but is logically distinct: the implication 'simple + non-abelian $\Rightarrow$ non-solvable' is one-way (a simple non-abelian group has only itself as a composition factor, which is non-abelian). Solvable-but-non-abelian: $S_3$ (order 6, derived length 2), $S_4$ (order 24, derived length 3), $A_4$ (order 12, contains $V_4 \trianglelefteq A_4$). Non-solvable-and-non-abelian: $S_5$ (order 120, contains $A_5$ as a simple composition factor), $A_5$ (order 60, the minimal simple non-abelian obstruction).

title: Galois Group Order Equals Extension Degree
content:
The `GaloisProperties` section (Part V, lines 221–235) establishes the fundamental numerical form of Galois theory. `galois_group_order`: for a finite Galois extension $E/F$, the order of the automorphism group $|\text{Aut}(E/F)|$ equals the extension degree $[E:F]$. This is `IsGalois.card_aut_eq_finrank` — the fundamental theorem of Galois theory stated numerically.

**Provenance — Artin's reformulation**: This identity is due to Emil Artin (1942), who reformulated classical Galois theory by *defining* a Galois extension as a finite extension $E/F$ for which $|\text{Aut}(E/F)| = [E:F]$, and then proving normality and separability follow. In Mathlib's `IsGalois` typeclass, the equivalence runs the other way (`IsGalois` is defined as normal + separable), and `card_aut_eq_finrank` is the derived numerical consequence — but Artin's perspective explains why this is the *fundamental* theorem: it captures the entire Galois correspondence in one cardinality identity. The Galois correspondence (subfields ↔ subgroups) is then a structural lifting of the numerical equality $|\text{Gal}(E/F)| = [E:F]$ to an inclusion-reversing bijection between subfields and subgroups.

**Source of the $\leq$ direction — Dedekind's linear independence of characters**: The inequality $|\text{Aut}(E/F)| \leq [E:F]$ holds for *every* finite extension (not just Galois) and is a consequence of **Dedekind's lemma** (1894): distinct field homomorphisms $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_m : E \to L$ are linearly independent as functions $E \to L$ when viewed as elements of the $L$-vector space of functions. Since $E$ has dimension $[E:F]$ over $F$ and the $\sigma_i$ are $F$-linear, at most $[E:F]$ of them can be linearly independent — bounding the number of $F$-automorphisms. The Galois condition (normal + separable) is exactly what forces the *equality*: separability gives enough distinct automorphisms; normality keeps them all inside $E$. Mathlib's `LinearIndependent.linear_independent_monoidHom` proves Dedekind's lemma in full generality (for monoid homomorphisms into a field), making `card_aut_eq_finrank` ultimately a corollary of linear algebra rather than abstract Galois theory.

**Abel-Ruffini application**: A quintic with Galois group $S_5$ necessarily generates a degree-120 extension (since $|S_5| = 120$). Each step of a radical tower $F_0 \subset F_1 \subset \cdots \subset F_k$ adjoins an $n$-th root and contributes a *cyclic* factor (after adjoining roots of unity) to the composition series — so the radical tower's Galois group has all-abelian composition factors. But $S_5$'s composition series $\{e\} \trianglelefteq A_5 \trianglelefteq S_5$ has the non-abelian simple factor $A_5$ of order 60. The numerical identity rules out radical towers by counting: there is no cyclic-factor decomposition of a 120-element group whose composition factors are all prime cyclic — the unique non-trivial composition factor of $A_5$ is $A_5$ itself.

**Hypotheses**: The theorem requires both `FiniteDimensional F E` (the extension has finite degree) and `IsGalois F E` (the extension is normal and separable). Removing either breaks the equality: for a non-normal extension like $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb{Q}$ (degree 3), $|\text{Aut}| = 1$ (only the identity, since the other two cube roots are non-real), strictly less than $[E:F] = 3$. For an inseparable extension over a field of characteristic $p$, the Frobenius collapses Galois orbits and again $|\text{Aut}| < [E:F]$. The Galois condition is precisely the hypothesis that makes the Lagrange inequality $|\text{Aut}(E/F)| \leq [E:F]$ an equality.

**Numerical bridge**: The result enables computing Galois group orders from extension degrees and vice versa: if $[E:\mathbb{Q}] = 120$ and $E/\mathbb{Q}$ is Galois, then $|\text{Gal}(E/\mathbb{Q})| = 120$. Combined with the classification that $S_n$ is not solvable for $n \geq 5$ (and $|S_5| = 120$), this provides the arithmetic bridge from the degree of a polynomial to the solvability of its Galois group, completing the chain: polynomial degree → splitting field degree → Galois group order → solvability classification.
mathContext:
$|\text{Gal}(E/F)| = [E:F]$ for finite Galois extensions. Equivalently: `Nat.card (E ≃ₐ[F] E) = Module.finrank F E`. Consequence: for a degree-$n$ irreducible polynomial $f$ with splitting field $E$ and Galois extension $E/\mathbb{Q}$, the Galois group $\text{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q}) \leq S_n$ has order dividing $n!$. If the extension degree equals $n!$, the Galois group is all of $S_n$.

**Formalized witness — `abel-ruffini-oq-04-oq-01`.** The companion gallery entry establishes exactly this scenario for the quintic $x^5 - 4x + 2$: it proves Eisenstein-at-$p=2$ irreducibility (forcing $[\mathbb{Q}(\alpha):\mathbb{Q}] = 5$) and `galActionHom` bijectivity (the action of $\text{Gal}(f/\mathbb{Q})$ on the 5 roots is faithful and transitive, so $\text{Gal} \hookrightarrow S_5$). Combined with a complex-conjugation transposition + a 5-cycle from irreducibility-mod-2 reduction, the embedding is surjective: $\text{Gal}(x^5 - 4x + 2 / \mathbb{Q}) \cong S_5$ exactly, with 0 sorries and 0 axioms. The splitting field's degree is then $120 = |S_5|$ by `card_aut_eq_finrank`'s converse direction, giving the file's largest concrete invocation of this identity: a degree-120 Galois extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ on which `not_solvable_by_rad_of_not_solvable_galois` (the gallery's contrapositive theorem of this entry's `Part IV`) certifies the roots are not expressible by radicals.

title: Group Order Computations: $|S_n| = n!$ and $|A_n| = n!/2$ for $n \leq 6$
content:
Thirteen computational theorems verify the group orders of symmetric and alternating groups for small $n$. For $n \leq 5$, `decide` suffices — exhaustive enumeration over the fintype is fast enough for the kernel evaluator. For $n = 6$ (720 and 360 elements), `native_decide` is required since the fintype is too large for kernel-time computation. The formula $|S_n| = n!$ reflects the definition of $S_n$ as the group of all bijections on an $n$-element set: there are $n!$ ways to arrange $n$ elements. The formula $|A_n| = n!/2$ follows from $A_n$ being an index-2 subgroup (via the sign homomorphism $\text{sign}: S_n \to \{\pm 1\}$). These cardinalities are not just bookkeeping: $|A_5| = 60$ is the smallest possible order for a non-abelian simple group, a fact that constrains the entire classification theory of finite simple groups.

**Why $|A_5|=60$ is the smallest non-abelian simple order — Burnside's $p^a q^b$ theorem (1904)**: For any group $G$ of order $p^a q^b$ where $p, q$ are primes, $G$ is solvable. So a non-abelian simple group must have order divisible by at least *three* distinct primes. The orders less than 60 divisible by three distinct primes are exactly $30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ and $42 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7$; both yield only solvable groups by Sylow-counting (the order-30 case: $n_5 \in \{1, 6\}$ forces a normal Sylow 5-subgroup; the order-42 case: $n_7 = 1$ forces a normal Sylow 7-subgroup). Thus 60 is the *minimum* possible order, and $A_5$ realizes it. The next non-abelian simple is $\mathrm{PSL}(2, 7) = \mathrm{GL}(3, 2)$ of order 168, then $A_6$ of order 360 — a sparse spectrum dictated by Sylow arithmetic before CFSG.

**The $|S_5|=120$ — $|A_6|=360$ band as the kernel-evaluator threshold**: This file's `decide` regime tops out at $|S_5| = 120$ (`card_s5`) and $|A_5| = 60$; `native_decide` is forced beginning at $|A_6| = 360$ (`card_a6`) and $|S_6| = 720$ (`card_s6`). The Lean kernel evaluator performs *whnf-driven* reduction with explicit `Acc` recursion unfolding — exponentially costly on `Equiv.Perm`-sized fintypes once the Cayley-table enumeration of $n!$ elements times $n!$ pairs (for binary operations) exceeds roughly $10^5$. The 120-vs-360 boundary in this file is the empirical inflection point; with native compilation, group-order computations remain tractable through $|S_8| = 40320$ (Part XIV `card_s8`). The *decision* between `decide` and `native_decide` is therefore not arbitrary but a verification-engineering choice that trades *trust-base size* (kernel-only vs kernel+compiler) for *per-theorem build time*.

**The index-2 identity and Lagrange's theorem**: $|A_n| = n!/2$ is the direct consequence of $A_n = \ker(\mathrm{sign})$ being an index-2 normal subgroup (Lagrange: $|S_n| = |A_n| \cdot [S_n : A_n] = |A_n| \cdot 2$ for $n \geq 2$), with the sign homomorphism $S_n \twoheadrightarrow \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ surjective for $n \geq 2$. The orbit-stabilizer theorem provides the structural justification for $|S_n| = n!$ itself: $S_n$ acts transitively on $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ with stabilizer $S_{n-1}$, giving $|S_n| = n \cdot |S_{n-1}|$, recursively yielding $n!$.

Values: $|S_2|=2, |S_3|=6, |S_4|=24, |S_5|=120, |S_6|=720$; $|A_0|=|A_1|=|A_2|=1, |A_3|=3, |A_4|=12, |A_5|=60, |A_6|=360$. The index-2 identity follows from Lagrange: $|S_n| = |A_n| \cdot [S_n:A_n] = |A_n| \cdot 2$. The orbit-stabilizer recurrence $|S_n| = n \cdot |S_{n-1}|$ gives $|S_n| = n!$ inductively. **Burnside's $p^a q^b$ theorem**: any group of order $p^a q^b$ is solvable, so a non-abelian simple group requires $\geq 3$ distinct prime factors; the minimum such order below 60 ($30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ and $42 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7$) admits only solvable groups by Sylow analysis, leaving $|A_5| = 60 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$ as the genuine minimum non-abelian simple order.

title: Part XI: Concrete Non-Solvability Witnesses for S₅–S₈ and A₆–A₇
content:
Six named one-liner theorems instantiating the general non-solvability results of Parts II and VII at specific small $n$: `s5_not_solvable`, `s6_not_solvable`, `s7_not_solvable`, `s8_not_solvable` for the symmetric side (lines 373–387), and `a6_not_solvable`, `a7_not_solvable` for the alternating side (lines 389–395). Each is a direct application of `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le` or `alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le` — the *general* `n ≥ 5` theorems established in Parts II and VII — to a specific small $n$, with the side condition $5 \leq n$ discharged by `le_rfl` (when $n = 5$) or `by omega` (when $n > 5$). Note: `a5_not_solvable` is *not* repeated here; it is established once in Part X (IndexTheorems, line 362) as `alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le le_rfl` and re-exported under that canonical name. The structural reverse-direction lemma `symmetric_not_solvable_of_alternating` (lines 397–403) closes the section and is annotated separately under `arg-symmetric-from-alternating`.

**Why six named one-liners instead of inlining the general theorem at use sites.** Each of these six named theorems is a *citation handle* — a named result downstream proofs can apply via `exact s5_not_solvable` rather than `exact symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le le_rfl`. The pattern is canonical in mathlib: a general theorem of the form `∀ n, 5 ≤ n → P n` plus specific corollaries `s5 : P 5`, `s6 : P 6`, etc. is preferred over forcing every call site to discharge the `5 ≤ n` side condition, because (a) the corollaries integrate with Lean's `simp` and `exact?` automation by name (a `simp [s5_not_solvable]` directive does not require pattern-matching on the universally-quantified general theorem), (b) the corollaries are typed for direct unification (`¬ IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin 5))` is a syntactically simpler goal than `¬ IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin ?n))` with metavariable), and (c) the corollaries provide *anchor points* for documentation and search — `#check s5_not_solvable` is more discoverable than the general theorem. This is the same pattern as Mathlib's `Nat.succ_pos` (specific consequence of `Nat.zero_lt_succ`) and the file's own `card_s2`, `card_s3`, ..., `card_s6` (Part VIII) and `card_s7`, `card_s8`, `card_a7`, `card_a8` (Part XIV).

**The Part XI / Part XIV redundancy and what distinguishes them.** Part XIV (lines 470–494) re-proves `a6_not_solvable_explicit` and `a7_not_solvable_explicit` *alongside* the high-cardinality witnesses |S₇|=5040, |S₈|=40320, |A₇|=2520, |A₈|=20160 and the new `a8_not_solvable`. The Part XIV `_explicit` suffix marks the *intentional duplication* — Part XI establishes the citation handles at the structural level (immediately after the general theorems they instantiate), while Part XIV groups the non-solvability witnesses *with* the cardinality verifications for $|S_7|, |S_8|, |A_7|, |A_8|$ that lift the file's `native_decide` regime above the 720-element kernel boundary first crossed at $|S_6|=720$ in Part VIII. The two are not strictly redundant: Part XIV adds `a8_not_solvable` (a seventh witness, not in Part XI) and the four explicit cardinality theorems. The redundant `_explicit` names ensure that Part XIV is *self-contained* as a 'high-cardinality bundle' — a reader who only loads Part XIV's `native_decide` results gets the non-solvability witnesses for $A_6, A_7, A_8$ alongside their orders, without back-reference to Part XI's `symmetric_not_solvable_of_five_le` instantiations. This dual-presentation is the file's house style for any result whose 'natural home' is one section but whose 'computational packaging' belongs to another.

**Cycle-index polynomial perspective — Frobenius's combinatorial accounting underneath the Lean witnesses.** Each of the six witnesses here is a statement about a permutation group whose conjugacy-class structure is fully captured by the **cycle-index polynomial** $Z(G) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} \prod_{k \geq 1} a_k^{c_k(g)}$ where $c_k(g)$ is the number of $k$-cycles in $g$'s cycle decomposition (Frobenius 1900, used implicitly in Pólya enumeration 1937). For $S_n$ the cycle index $Z(S_n)$ is the elementary symmetric function $h_n(a_1, a_2, \ldots)$ in the power-sum-to-monomial basis transformation; for $A_n$ the index is $Z(A_n) = \frac{1}{2}[Z(S_n) + Z'(S_n)]$ where $Z'$ flips signs on cycles of even length (Burnside 1911, Pólya 1937). The conjugacy classes of $S_5$, indexed by partitions of 5 ($1^5, 1^3 2, 1 2^2, 1^2 3, 1 4, 5, 2 3$) with sizes 1, 10, 15, 20, 30, 24, 20 = 120, are the **combinatorial atoms** that any solvability check must navigate; the simplicity of $A_5$ proved by `alternatingGroup.isSimpleGroup_five` is equivalent to the assertion that the *only* normal subgroup of $A_5$ is generated by a union of full conjugacy classes summing to 1 or 60 — and the conjugacy-class sizes of $A_5$ ($1, 12, 12, 15, 20$) admit no proper subset summing to a divisor of 60 other than $\{1\}$, which is exactly the Sylow-counting argument cited in this entry's keyInsight #8 reformulated as a partition-arithmetic constraint. Thus each of the six Lean witnesses here ($s_5, s_6, s_7, s_8, a_6, a_7$ not solvable) is the *typeclass-level shadow* of the conjugacy-class arithmetic that establishes the underlying simplicity result — Frobenius's 1900 character-theoretic apparatus translates directly into Mathlib's `inferInstance` derivations once the simple-group classification is loaded.

Containment chain: $A_5 \leq A_6 \leq A_7 \leq \ldots$ All $A_n$ for $n \geq 5$ contain the non-abelian simple group $A_5$ as a subgroup (via the natural embedding fixing $\{6, \ldots, n\}$), so all inherit non-solvability by subgroup closure. Symmetrically $S_n \supseteq A_n$, so $A_n$ not solvable $\Rightarrow S_n$ not solvable (contrapositive of subgroup closure). The six witnesses here unwind these abstract containments at specific $n \in \{5, 6, 7, 8\}$ (symmetric) and $n \in \{6, 7\}$ (alternating).

**Conjugacy-class arithmetic for $A_5$:** the five classes have sizes $\{1, 12, 12, 15, 20\}$, with the two size-12 classes being the *split* of the 24-element conjugacy class of $5$-cycles in $S_5$ under $A_5$ (a phenomenon: a conjugacy class of $S_n$ that lies in $A_n$ may split into two $A_n$-classes when its centralizer in $S_n$ is contained in $A_n$). The simplicity of $A_5$ is equivalent to: no proper non-empty subset $S$ of $\{1, 12, 12, 15, 20\}$ containing $1$ satisfies $\sum S \mid 60$. Direct enumeration: $1, 1+12=13, 1+15=16, 1+20=21, 1+12+12=25, 1+12+15=28, \ldots$ — *none* of these is a non-trivial divisor of 60 (the divisors are $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60\}$), so the only normal subgroups are $\{e\}$ and $A_5$. This is the *combinatorial heart* of all six non-solvability witnesses in this section.
