title: Structural Reverse-Direction: A_n Non-Solvable ⟹ S_n Non-Solvable
content: Theorem `symmetric_not_solvable_of_alternating` (lines 397–403) isolates the *structural* one-directional implication: from `¬ IsSolvable (alternatingGroup (Fin n))` we conclude `¬ IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))`. The proof is striking in its brevity — `intro hsol; exact h inferInstance` — three tokens that compress a substantial mathematical fact: **subgroups of solvable groups are solvable**. The `inferInstance` call wakes up Mathlib's typeclass resolution to discharge `IsSolvable (alternatingGroup (Fin n))` *given* `IsSolvable (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))`, using the universal lemma `Subgroup.isSolvable`. The hypothesis `h` then contradicts this derived instance. Pedagogically this isolates *which* direction of the iff requires structural group theory: the forward (`S_n` solvable ⟹ `A_n` solvable) is structural and free; the reverse (`A_n` solvable ⟹ `S_n` solvable) requires the genuine work in Parts I–IV of this file, because $S_n / A_n \cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ must independently be solvable (it is — trivially abelian — but proving it composes correctly with the kernel is the content of `solvable_of_ker_le_range`).
mathContext: Subgroup-of-solvable-is-solvable: if $G$ is solvable with derived series $G^{(0)} \supseteq G^{(1)} \supseteq \cdots \supseteq \{e\}$ terminating at length $k$, and $H \leq G$, then $H^{(i)} \leq G^{(i)}$ for all $i$, so $H^{(k)} = \{e\}$ and $H$ is solvable. Applied to $A_n \leq S_n$: $S_n$ solvable ⟹ $A_n$ solvable (free). The contrapositive: $A_n$ not solvable ⟹ $S_n$ not solvable. Notation: $G^{(k+1)} = [G^{(k)}, G^{(k)}]$ is the iterated commutator subgroup.

title: Part XIV: Higher Cardinalities and Extended Non-Solvability (S₇, S₈, A₇, A₈)
content:
Part XIV extends the cardinality computation to $S_7$, $S_8$, $A_7$, $A_8$ (all requiring `native_decide`) and adds three explicit non-solvability results: $A_6$, $A_7$, $A_8$ not solvable. All non-solvability results are one-liner applications of `alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le (by omega)`. The key mathematical fact is that non-solvability propagates upward through containment: $A_5 \leq A_6 \leq A_7 \leq A_8 \leq \ldots$, and any group containing a non-solvable subgroup is itself non-solvable (subgroup solvability contraposes). The exceptional isomorphism $A_8 \cong GL_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ connects this algebraic computation to the classification of finite simple groups — both groups have order 20160, and this is one of five exceptional isomorphisms between alternating groups and classical groups over $\mathbb{F}_2$ discovered during the classification effort.

**The five exceptional isomorphisms — a complete enumeration.** The classification of finite simple groups (CFSG, completed 2004) catalogs every finite non-abelian simple group as either (i) cyclic of prime order, (ii) alternating $A_n$ for $n \geq 5$, (iii) a group of Lie type (e.g. $\mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{F}_q)$, $\mathrm{PSp}_{2n}(\mathbb{F}_q)$, $\mathrm{P\Omega}^\pm_{2n}(\mathbb{F}_q)$, $G_2(\mathbb{F}_q)$, etc.), or (iv) one of the 26 sporadic groups. The alternating and Lie-type families *almost never* overlap — but exactly **five exceptional coincidences** appear among the smallest cases, three of which involve groups discussed in this file:

  - $A_5 \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_4) \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_5)$ (order $60$ — *double* coincidence at the minimal non-abelian simple group)
  - $A_6 \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_9)$ (order $360$)
  - $A_8 \cong \mathrm{PSL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2) = \mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (order $20160$ — the largest coincidence, established here)
  - $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_7) \cong \mathrm{PSL}_3(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (order $168$ — *not* an alternating group; the second-smallest non-abelian simple group)

No further coincidences exist: for $n \geq 9$, $A_n$ is *not* isomorphic to any $\mathrm{PSL}_k(\mathbb{F}_q)$ or other classical group of Lie type. The five exceptional isomorphisms are therefore not a generic pattern but a finite exceptional phenomenon at the *bottom* of the simple-group hierarchy — the same numerical regime where the solvability classification in this file lives.

**Why $A_8 \cong \mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ — a concrete construction.** Note that for $\mathbb{F}_2$, the determinant map $\det : \mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2) \to \mathbb{F}_2^\times = \{1\}$ is trivially surjective onto the one-element group, so $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2) = \mathrm{SL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2) = \mathrm{PSL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (the center is also trivial in characteristic 2 since the only scalar in $\mathbb{F}_2^\times$ is $1$). The isomorphism $A_8 \cong \mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ comes from an explicit action: $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts faithfully on the *non-zero vectors* of $\mathbb{F}_2^4 \setminus \{0\}$ (a 15-element set), and this action extends to a permutation representation on the eight cosets of a specific point stabilizer — yielding an embedding $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2) \hookrightarrow S_8$. Since both groups have order $20160$, the embedding is forced to land in $A_8$ (as a counting argument: only one index-2 subgroup of $S_8$ exists). The geometric interpretation: $\mathbb{F}_2^4$ has 15 non-zero vectors and 35 lines through the origin (3-element subsets closed under addition); the 35 lines partition into a *Steiner system* $S(3, 4, 8)$, and $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts on this 8-block structure as $A_8$. This is Witt's 1938 construction. The same circle of ideas yields $\mathrm{Sp}_6(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acting on the $2 \cdot 28 = 56$ trisecant lines of a Fermat curve — another classical accident vanishing for higher-rank groups.

**Geometric interpretations of the smaller coincidences.**
  - **$A_5 \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_5)$**: arises from $A_5$'s action on the projective line $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_5) = \mathbb{F}_5 \cup \{\infty\}$ (a 6-point set). The action permutes the six points via $z \mapsto (az + b)/(cz + d)$ for $\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_5)$. The kernel is trivial in $\mathrm{PSL}_2$, so the action gives an embedding $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_5) \hookrightarrow S_6$; counting (both orders $60$) forces the image to be $A_5 \leq A_6 \leq S_6$. This is **the icosahedral isomorphism** featured in this file's keyInsight #6.
  - **$A_5 \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_4)$**: $\mathbb{F}_4 = \{0, 1, \omega, \omega^2\}$ has $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_4)$ of size 5, and $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_4)$ acts faithfully on this 5-point set, yielding $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_4) \hookrightarrow S_5$, again forced to $A_5$ by counting. This explains why $A_5$ is the *first* member of *two* infinite families ($\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_q)$ for $q \in \{4, 5\}$): the alternating-group structure is the intersection.
  - **$A_6 \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_9)$**: arises from the unique non-trivial *outer automorphism* of $A_6$ (the only outer automorphism among all alternating groups for $n \neq 6$). $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_9)$ acts on $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_9)$ (10 points); restricting to the action on a particular set of six special points gives $A_6$. The exceptional outer automorphism of $A_6$ is itself a famously bizarre feature — the unique counterexample to 'every alternating group has trivial outer automorphism group for $n \neq 2, 6$' (Hölder 1895).
  - **$\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_7) \cong \mathrm{PSL}_3(\mathbb{F}_2)$**: order $168$. $\mathrm{PSL}_3(\mathbb{F}_2)$ acts on $\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (the Fano plane with 7 points and 7 lines, the smallest projective plane); $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_7)$ acts on $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_7)$ (8 points). The isomorphism is non-obvious but classical (Klein 1879).

**Why no more coincidences exist.** For $n \geq 9$, $A_n$ has order $n!/2$ which grows faster than the order of any $\mathrm{PSL}_k(\mathbb{F}_q)$ family at fixed $k$. More precisely: the order $|\mathrm{PSL}_k(\mathbb{F}_q)|$ is asymptotically $q^{k^2 - 1}$ (Lie-theoretic dimension counting), while $|A_n| \sim n!/2 \gg q^{k^2-1}$ for any fixed $k$ as $n \to \infty$. The only way a Lie-type group of large order can coincide with $A_n$ is if $k$ grows logarithmically with $n$, but the specific orders never match. The classification of finite simple groups (Aschbacher 1986–2004 confirmation) verified there are *exactly* the four families listed, plus the $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_7) \cong \mathrm{PSL}_3(\mathbb{F}_2)$ non-alternating coincidence.

**Tactic mechanics: `native_decide` vs `decide` at $|S_8| = 40320$.** The Lean tactic `decide` reduces a decidable proposition to its `Bool` value via the *kernel evaluator*, which uses term reduction and has built-in safety limits (heap budget, deduction step budget). For `Fintype.card (Equiv.Perm (Fin 8)) = 40320`, the kernel would need to enumerate all 40320 permutations and check equality — feasible algorithmically but exceeding the kernel's default budget. The `native_decide` tactic instead *compiles* the decidable proposition to native code (via Lean's compiler to Lean's IR, then to OCaml runtime, then to native), runs it, and trusts the result. The trade-off: `decide` produces a proof term checkable by the trusted kernel; `native_decide` produces a proof term trusting the compiled binary's output. For order computations on large fintypes, `native_decide` is the standard pattern. The cardinality theorems here ($|S_7|, |S_8|, |A_7|, |A_8|$) are all in this regime, while $|S_5|, |A_5|, |S_6|, |A_6|$ in Part VIII still fall within `decide`'s reach (or borderline; some Part VIII proofs already use `native_decide` to be safe). The boundary between `decide` and `native_decide` in this file is therefore at approximately $|G| \approx 360$–$720$, with $S_6$ and $A_6$ already requiring native compilation.

**Connection to the file's central threshold.** The cardinality computations $|A_7| = 2520, |A_8| = 20160$ and the parallel non-solvability witnesses $A_7, A_8$ unsolvable are *not* deeper mathematical content beyond Part III ($A_5$ simple, $A_5$ unsolvable) — they propagate from the $A_5$ obstruction by subgroup-closure of solvability (contrapositive: $A_5 \leq A_n$ for $n \geq 5$, so if $A_n$ were solvable, $A_5$ would inherit solvability, contradicting Part III). What Part XIV adds is *computational verification* that Mathlib's `Fintype.card` API correctly handles cardinalities up to 40320 and that the abstract non-solvability theorems instantiate cleanly at $n = 6, 7, 8$ — a regression-test layer ensuring the file's main biconditionals work uniformly across the $n \geq 5$ regime, not just at the boundary $n = 5$.
mathContext:
$|S_7| = 7! = 5040$; $|S_8| = 8! = 40320$; $|A_7| = 7!/2 = 2520$; $|A_8| = 8!/2 = 20160$. Exceptional: $A_8 \cong \mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2) = \mathrm{SL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2) = \mathrm{PSL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (the group of invertible $4 \times 4$ matrices over $\mathbb{F}_2$, also order 20160; in characteristic 2 with $\mathbb{F}_2^\times = \{1\}$, $\mathrm{GL} = \mathrm{SL} = \mathrm{PSL}$ trivially). Non-solvability chain: $A_5 \hookrightarrow A_6 \hookrightarrow A_7 \hookrightarrow A_8$, so $A_n$ not solvable for all $n \geq 5$ (by `alternating_not_solvable_of_five_le`). `native_decide` compiles to native code — required since $|S_8| = 40320$ elements exceed the kernel reduction budget.

**Complete exceptional-isomorphism table for $A_n$ and finite simple Lie-type groups (all that exist):**

| $n$ | $A_n$ | $\cong$ | Order | Geometric interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | $A_5$ | $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_4) \cong \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_5)$ | 60 | Icosahedral rotations; $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_4)$ (5 points) and $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_5)$ (6 points) |
| 6 | $A_6$ | $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_9)$ | 360 | Action on $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{F}_9)$ (10 points); related to outer automorphism of $A_6$ |
| 8 | $A_8$ | $\mathrm{GL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2) = \mathrm{PSL}_4(\mathbb{F}_2)$ | 20160 | Action on $\mathbb{F}_2^4 \setminus \{0\}$ (15 vectors) and the Steiner system $S(3,4,8)$ |

Plus one *non-alternating* exceptional coincidence: $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_7) \cong \mathrm{PSL}_3(\mathbb{F}_2)$ (order 168, action on the Fano plane). No further coincidences exist (proved as a consequence of CFSG order-counting).

**Order asymptotics ruling out further coincidences:** $|A_n| \sim \sqrt{2\pi n} (n/e)^n / 2$ by Stirling; $|\mathrm{PSL}_k(\mathbb{F}_q)| \sim q^{k^2 - 1}$ for fixed $k$. The ratio $|A_n| / |\mathrm{PSL}_k(\mathbb{F}_q)| \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$ for any fixed $(k, q)$, so coincidences are confined to small parameter regions. The Aschbacher-O'Nan-Scott theorem (1986) catalogs all primitive permutation actions of $A_n$, sealing the no-more-coincidences result.

title: Part XV: Factorial Identity Verification ($|S_n| = n!$ and $|A_n| = n!/2$)
content:
Part XV formally proves the factorial identities connecting `Fintype.card` to `Nat.factorial`. `factorial_s3/s4/s5` verify $|S_n| = n!$ for $n = 3, 4, 5$; `half_factorial_a3/a4/a5` verify $|A_n| = n!/2$ for $n = 3, 4, 5$. All use `decide` (small enough for kernel evaluation). These serve as simp lemmas bridging the abstract group-order API to concrete arithmetic, enabling downstream calculations. Integer division $n!/2$ is always exact for $n \geq 2$ since $A_n$ has index 2 in $S_n$ (the sign homomorphism is surjective). These identities also function as regression tests confirming that Mathlib's `Fintype.card (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))` correctly evaluates to $n!$ — a non-trivial fact since the definition works via fintype instances, not direct enumeration.

**Combinatorial cycle-type interpretation**: each $\sigma \in S_n$ decomposes uniquely into disjoint cycles whose lengths form an (unordered) partition $\lambda \vdash n$.
